beats.narration_text: Part one: the framework itself — four parts, the same everywhere.
Situation. Task. Action. Result. Situation sets the scene. Task is your responsibility in it. Action is what you specifically did. Result is the outcome — and what changed because of it.

show.event: four boxes land in sequence, S-T-A-R
each box's one-line definition fades in beneath it

production_viz.label: STAR
production_viz.note: matches Ch.12's own STAR structure diagram

beats.narration_text: The generic STAR failure is all Situation, no Result. Candidates set the scene, and never say what happened.

beats.narration_text: Part two: what a banking panel listens for, on top of the generic.

beats.act: II — What a Banking Panel Listens For
beats.narration_text: A banking panel is listening for three things the generic rubric doesn't name. Risk awareness — did you notice a problem before you were told about it. Regulatory and control judgment — did you understand why a rule existed, not just that it did. And comfort under audit or examiner scrutiny — can you describe defending your work without sounding defensive.

show.event: three panels land one at a time
all three settle side by side

production_viz.label: competencies
production_viz.note: risk awareness / regulatory-control judgment / audit-examiner comfort, Ch.12

beats.act: II — What a Banking Panel Listens For
beats.narration_text: Three situations show up often enough to prepare a story for each. Flagging a data-quality issue before it reaches a report. Working through an internal-audit or examiner-style request. And navigating conflicting pressure between a business stakeholder and a control function.

chips: Survive an audit or examiner request

beats.act: II — What a Banking Panel Listens For
beats.narration_text: Here's the banking-specific failure. 'I noticed the numbers looked off' is not a Result a risk-aware panel accepts. 'I flagged it to my lead before it went into the report, and we caught the error before quarter-end close' is.

props.after: "I flagged it to my lead before it reached the report — we caught the error before quarter-end close."

beats.act: II — What a Banking Panel Listens For
beats.narration_text: And when you deliver it, be specific. 'We fixed it' is weaker than 'we added a validation check that catches that specific error before it reaches the report.' The second version proves you understood why the problem mattered — not just that you solved it once.

show.event: strong phrase lands in its place

production_viz.note: same visual grammar as the SQL video's B08_CorrectedBalance

beats.narration_text: Part three: a weak answer, and the STAR rewrite.

beats.role_note: the weak answer (quoted verbatim from the book)
beats.narration_text: "Yeah, actually one time I found a mistake in a report a coworker made. The numbers were off. I mentioned it and we fixed it before it went out. It worked out fine."

props.eyebrow: "TELL ME ABOUT A TIME YOU FOUND AN ERROR…"
props.quote: "Yeah, actually one time I found a mistake in a report a coworker made. The numbers were off. I mentioned it and we fixed it before it went out. It worked out fine."

beats.role_note: the STAR rewrite (quoted/paraphrased verbatim from the book)
beats.narration_text: Situation: reviewing a monthly revenue-by-region dashboard, two days before it reaches the VP of Sales. Task: not formally assigned to QA it — but this is the data model underneath it. Action: one region's numbers had roughly doubled with no business reason — traced to a schema change, flagged the same day, the publish held until it's confirmed. Result: the VP never sees the bad number, and a data-quality check goes into the dbt test suite, so the same bug can't reach a report undetected again.

cards.label: Situation
cards.detail: Reviewing a monthly revenue-by-region dashboard, two days before it reaches the VP of Sales.

cards.label: Task
cards.detail: Not formally assigned to QA it — but built the underlying data model it pulled from.

cards.label: Action
cards.detail: Traced a doubled region to a schema change, flagged it same-day, held the publish for confirmation.

cards.label: Result
cards.detail: The VP never saw the bad number — a dbt test now catches it automatically.

beats.narration_text: Three things get scored here. Risk awareness — treating 'is this plausible' as a check worth running. Escalation — raising it immediately, to the right people. Outcome — naming the specific control that now exists because of the incident.

beats.narration_text: Part four: Daniel's full-loop mock — stage four.

A realistic banking loop runs five stages back to back. Domain vocabulary. SQL. Case. Behavioral. Systems design. Daniel — three and a half years into his analyst career — runs all five in one sitting, under time pressure. Stage four is behavioral.

show.event: five boxes land left to right

beats.role_note: the prompt (quoted verbatim from the book)
beats.narration_text: "Tell me about a time you found an error in your own or a colleague's work."

props.quote: "Tell me about a time you found an error in your own or a colleague's work."

beats.role_note: Daniel's answer, where it stops (paraphrased/quoted from the book)
beats.narration_text: Daniel describes finding a mis-joined table that inflated a retention metric. Then he stops: 'I fixed it and let my manager know.' No new check. No changed process. No number.

props.quote: "…I fixed it and let my manager know."

beats.role_note: the score, and the pattern across the other four stages
beats.narration_text: Scored against the book's own rubric: a one. STAR shape — but no named escalation, no named control, no stated outcome. And Daniel's not alone up there — his other four stages all landed the same one place short of a three.

beats.narration_text: Behavioral is Daniel's only one — it gets the bulk of his remaining hours. His four twos share one gap: correct, but missing the final detail that makes it a three. His lesson for himself: finish the thought out loud.

show.event: calendar/allocation bars build, most hours on Behavioral

beats.narration_text: The STAR method doesn't change in a bank. What a bank panel is listening for in the Result does: name the control, name the escalation, or the story doesn't score — no matter how real it is.

artifactLines: The STAR shape is universal — Situation, Task, Action, Result.
A bank panel scores the Result differently: name the control, name the escalation.
Daniel's mock proves it — correct answers, no credit, until the thought finishes out loud.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — prompt read aloud and discussed, not just shown
beats.narration_text: Your move: draft one STAR story for a time you flagged a problem before being asked to. Situation, Task, Action — then don't stop at 'and I fixed it.' Name exactly who you told, when, and what changed as a result.
